KEY MESSAGE 1... 
The combination of a low-level trough axis and modest warm air/
moisture advection has been fueling some thunderstorms early
this morning, primarily over Lake Erie but extending southwest
into parts of North Central OH as of 3 AM. While this activity
is generally favored to lift east-northeast and diminish this
morning, it may still be on the scope as the rest of the world
awakens, particularly over and close to Lake Erie. While it may
not be an entirely dry morning given this activity, greater 
shower and storm potential, including a risk for some strong to 
severe storms, awaits until the afternoon and evening hours. 

Aloft, a shortwave will dig into the central Great Lakes today
into tonight while taking on a neutral to slightly negative
tilt. This will encourage a weak surface low to slowly deepen
while drifting out of northern Michigan and into southern
Ontario late today and tonight. A pre-frontal trough is still
expected to cross the area this afternoon and early evening from
west to east, with a strong cold front arriving in Northwest OH
late this afternoon and surging southeast across the area
through this evening. Large scale forcing for ascent will
maximize late this afternoon and evening as a vort max rounds
the base of the deepening shortwave and rotates into the
northern OH/Lake Erie vicinity, though more modest forcing is
evident even earlier in the day. 

Showers/storms are expected to begin developing during the
midday or early afternoon timeframe, with activity peaking in
coverage, intensity, and organization during the late afternoon
and early evening. Showers/storms are expected to exit southeast
this evening with the cold front, with activity quickly
transitioning to lake-enhanced showers later tonight. Activity
will likely blossom along both the pre-frontal trough and a lake
breeze near the northeastern shoreline near and east of the I-77
corridor this afternoon, and across Northwest OH along the cold
front itself. Given the increasing forcing into the late 
afternoon/evening and multiple triggers for convection, it's 
likely that eastern portions of our area see the most widespread
convection and greatest overall rain amounts, with some areas 
likely seeing multiple rounds in quick succession. With that 
said, nearly all CAMs develop fairly numerous storms along the 
cold front as it pushes across our western counties, so odds are
that a large majority of the area will see a shower or storm 
this afternoon/evening on the balance. 

There is some potential for both severe weather and locally 
heavy rain with storms this afternoon/evening, though the
overall setup will not favor higher end convective hazards. 
Clouds and perhaps some ongoing shower/thunder activity will 
slow heating today, though weak to moderate, uncapped 
instability (1000-2000 J/KG of MLCAPE) is expected to develop 
through the afternoon as low-level lapse rates steepen to around
8C/km. Some pockets of dry air aloft will contribute to modest 
DCAPE values in the 500-800 J/KG range. These marginal 
thermodynamics, coupled with increasing forcing and modest deep-
layer shear values of 20-30kt, can support loosely organized 
convection. The primary severe threat today will be locally 
damaging winds, most likely with any small lines or clusters 
that evolve but also possible with any more intense cells. 
Isolated large hail is also possible, mainly with any updrafts 
that exhibit transient rotation which is most likely within 
storms along/east of the pre-frontal trough where surface flow 
will be more backed. While the overall lower-end environment and
potential for storms to quickly get "messy" and work over the 
atmosphere puts a lid on severe potential today, most CAMs have 
quite a bit of convection across our area with some organization
depicted, giving the SPC confidence to introduce a Slight Risk 
(level 2 of 5) for severe weather for much of the area east of 
the I-75 corridor (and a Marginal/level 1 of 5 for I-75). 

In terms of heavy rain potential, storm motions from the west- 
southwest will be fairly parallel to the incoming cold front, 
so the potential for multiple rounds and/or transient training 
does exist. Precipitable water values and warm cloud depths are 
not especially concerning for efficient rain-rates, though we 
will need to monitor portions of Northeast OH/Northwest PA for 
repeated storms or training convection that can still drop 
localized 2-3" rain amounts. Otherwise, area-average QPF will 
generally be in the 0.25-1.00" range through this evening, least
across Northwest OH and greatest across Northeast OH/Northwest 
PA. The WPC has introduced a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 4) for 
excessive rainfall/localized flash flooding across Northeast OH 
and Northwest PA in their latest excessive rainfall outlook.
